Amanda, thanks for coming early. The panel starts in twenty minutes, and you are the second of three speakers.
Thank you, Daniel. How long do I have to outline our position?
Four minutes, and then questions. Most of the audience are investors, so they will ask about integrity.
Then I will address that directly. The evidence suggests that buyers are becoming more careful.
Good. Let me try a hard one. Are Brazilian credits reliable or not?
Most of them are likely to be robust, but some projects may have weak baselines. We should be honest about that.
They will also ask about the new rules. Is there a loophole?
There seems to be one in how land use is counted. If nobody closes it, it could weaken the pledges made last year.
And who loses if nobody closes it? I want a real answer, not a slogan.
Local stakeholders, in most cases. That is why we need rules that mitigate the risk on the ground, not only on paper.

Good afternoon. I will be brief, because the negotiations are still going on. Three points. First, on carbon markets, we have made progress, but it is too early to say that we have an agreement. The text that was published this morning is likely to change again tonight. Second, several countries have asked for stronger rules on integrity. The evidence suggests that buyers will not return to the market until the rules are robust, and we agree with that. Third, on finance, the pledges that were made last year have not been fully delivered. It seems that some countries are waiting for the final text before they commit more money. We may see new announcements on Thursday, but I would not expect large numbers. I will take two questions.

When lawyers speak at an international forum, they often make one of two mistakes. The first is to sound too certain. If you say that a project will remove one million tons of carbon, somebody in the room will ask you to prove it, and you probably cannot. The second mistake is the opposite: to hedge everything. If every sentence starts with perhaps, or it might be possible that, the audience stops listening, because they cannot find your position. So use a simple structure. Start with your point, in one sentence, with no hedge. Then give the evidence, and this is where hedging belongs: the data suggests, the numbers seem to show. Then explain the impact: who is affected, and how. And finish with a recommendation, clear and short. Point, evidence, impact, recommendation. One hedge for each claim is enough. Two hedges in the same sentence sound like fear.

First, thank the moderator and say who you are. Then state your point in one sentence, with no hedge. Then give the evidence, with a careful verb such as suggests. Then explain the impact: who is affected, and how. And finally, finish with a clear recommendation.
